questions.citation_source: PubMed — PMID: 8627466 — "Physiology of growth hormone secretion during sleep" — J Pediatr — 1996

questions.question_text: Is one team sport enough to meet activity needs?
questions.answer_template: A single practice or game often does not cover every day, and it may lean toward one type of movement, so add active play and some impact activity on the other days. Variety also reduces overuse injury from repeating the same motion. Use the sport as a base and fill around it.
questions.citation_source: PubMed — PMID: 33239350 — "World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour" — Br J Sports Med — 2020

questions.question_text: How can I make activity a family habit?
questions.answer_template: Children copy what they see, so family walks, bike rides, games in the park and active weekends make movement normal and fun. Doing it together also builds the relationship. Habits set in childhood tend to carry into adult life.

questions.question_text: Is dance or gymnastics just as good for boys?
questions.answer_template: Absolutely — dance and gymnastics build impact-loaded bone strength, coordination, flexibility and body control that benefit any child regardless of gender. They are excellent athletic foundations that carry into other sports. Choose the activity by the child's interest, not by stereotype.

questions.question_text: What does martial-arts belt progression teach beyond fitness?
questions.answer_template: Alongside strength, balance and coordination, the belt system teaches goal-setting, patience, respect and self-discipline as a child earns each level. That structure keeps many children motivated and active for years. The life-skills side is a real part of the value.

questions.question_text: Are short sprint bursts better than long slow running for kids?
questions.answer_template: For bone, the higher ground forces of sprinting give more stimulus than steady jogging, and children naturally move in bursts anyway, so sprint games and intervals suit them well. Both build fitness; sprinting adds a bit more bone loading. Mix them into play rather than making a child run long distances.

questions.question_text: How do I keep a child who dislikes team sport active?
questions.answer_template: Lean into individual and playful options — swimming, cycling, martial arts, dance, climbing, running games, skateboarding or simply active outdoor play — so they can be active on their own terms. Enjoyment is what sustains the habit. The best activity is the one your child will actually keep doing.

questions.question_text: Does good posture relate to activity and looking taller?
questions.answer_template: Core and back strength from activity, plus not slouching over screens, help a child hold their full height and move well — posture does not change bone length but it changes how tall they stand and carry themselves. Activities like swimming, yoga, gymnastics and general play build the supporting muscles. Limiting long hunched screen time helps too.

questions.question_text: How much sitting is too much for a child?
questions.answer_template: Long unbroken sitting — long screen sessions in particular — is worth breaking up with movement, and guidelines advise limiting recreational sedentary time. Standing, stretching or a quick active burst every so often counters it. The aim is less prolonged sitting and more movement across the day.
questions.citation_source: PubMed — PMID: 33239350 — "World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour" — Br J Sports Med — 2020

questions.question_text: Is swimming still worth it if it does not build much bone?
questions.answer_template: Definitely — swimming builds cardiovascular fitness, whole-body muscle, lung capacity and is a vital safety skill, and it is ideal for joints and for heavier children. The only caveat is that it loads bone little, so pair it with some weight-bearing activity during the week. It is a superb activity, just not a standalone bone-builder.
questions.citation_source: PubMed — PMID: 23147022 — "Bone health in endurance athletes: runners, cyclists, and swimmers" — Curr Sports Med Rep — 2012

questions.question_text: Does being active outdoors give a vitamin D bonus for bones?
questions.answer_template: Yes — outdoor activity exposes skin to sunlight, the main way the body makes vitamin D, which bones need to use calcium, so outdoor play helps bone via loading AND vitamin D. Balance sensible sun time with sunburn protection. It is two bone benefits from one habit.

questions.question_text: What is a simple weekly activity plan for a growing child?
questions.answer_template: Aim for about an hour of activity most days, made of active play plus a sport or two, and make sure some of it is impact or weight-bearing (running, jumping, sport) on at least three days for bone. Fold in walking or cycling for transport, and protect sleep. Variety and enjoyment keep it going long-term.
questions.citation_source: PubMed — PMID: 33239350 — "World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour" — Br J Sports Med — 2020

questions.question_text: Do wearables and step counts help keep my child active?
questions.answer_template: Step or activity trackers can motivate some children by making movement visible and turning it into a game, and GrowSense logs activity to show whether the week included enough bone-loading types. They are a helper, not a requirement — the goal is enjoyable daily movement. Do not let a number replace fun.

questions.question_text: Is it okay for my child to be active every single day?
questions.answer_template: Yes — daily movement is healthy and recommended, provided intensity varies and there are easier days rather than maximal training every day. Children's play is naturally intermittent, which builds in recovery. Consistent, varied, enjoyable activity beats occasional intense sessions.

questions.question_text: Is a Thai Omelette (Kai Jeow) a good quick meal for kids?
questions.answer_template: Kai jeow is a fluffy fried egg omelette that delivers complete egg protein and yolk micronutrients over rice, and it is fast, mild and well accepted by children. It is pan-fried in oil, so drain it and keep the portion sensible. Adding minced pork or vegetables makes it a more complete plate.

questions.question_text: Is white rice or brown rice better for my growing child?
questions.answer_template: Both give the carbohydrate energy active children need; brown and other wholegrain rices add more fibre, B vitamins and minerals like magnesium for the same energy. A mix, or brown where the child accepts it, is ideal, but white rice is perfectly fine as the energy base alongside protein and vegetables. What sits on the rice matters more than the rice itself.

questions.question_text: Are soft or runny eggs safe for children?
questions.answer_template: Fully cooked eggs are safest for young children, since runny yolks and whites carry a small salmonella risk that little ones handle less well. Older children and pasteurized eggs lower that concern. When unsure, cook eggs through — the protein and nutrients are the same.

questions.question_text: What are the signs my child is doing too much sport?
questions.answer_template: Warning signs of overtraining include lingering fatigue, dropping performance, frequent niggling injuries, joint pain (especially near a growth plate), poor sleep and loss of enthusiasm. The fix is more rest, variety and adequate fuelling, not pushing harder. Persistent pain or a limp deserves a medical check rather than playing through it.

questions.question_text: Do playground swings and slides count as exercise?
questions.answer_template: They involve climbing, gripping, core control and bursts of movement, so unstructured playground time genuinely contributes to a young child's daily activity and motor development. Swinging builds core and coordination while ladders and slides add climbing. It is active play that counts toward the day's movement total.
